title: The Tiny Beginning
on_slide_text: Sage Valmiki has just heard from Narada about a perfect man full of truth and kindness. Narada has promised to tell his noble story. Now a very small moment by a river is about to grow into a very big book. Watch closely, for greatness often starts small.
rationale: Opens on the hook that a tiny river moment will birth a vast epic after Narada's promise.

title: Farewell Through Sky
on_slide_text: Valmiki folds his hands and honours Narada with flowers and sweet water. His young disciples stand beside him with love. Narada smiles and blesses them all. Then he rises into the bright sky and flies back to his own shining world.
rationale: Shows honoured farewell as Narada leaves through sky, closing the prior telling.

title: The Clean Riverbank
on_slide_text: Valmiki walks with Bharadwaja to the calm Tamasa river near Ganga. The water is clear and the bank is clean with no mud. Valmiki smiles at the pure spot. He says, dear child Bharadwaja, set down the water pot and bring my bark cloth for bathing.
rationale: Places Valmiki at Tamasa's clean bank and sets up the bathing request to Bharadwaja.

title: The Bark Cloth
on_slide_text: Bharadwaja quickly obeys his teacher and brings the soft bark cloth. Valmiki takes it with kind thanks. Before he steps into the water, he walks slowly among the green trees. He looks around at leaves, light, and life with happy eyes.
rationale: Shows obedient preparation and slow forest gaze before bathing.

title: Two Happy Birds
on_slide_text: Near a wide tree Valmiki sees two krauncha birds side by side. They are mates, singing sweet songs together. They hop and play with joy in the warm sun. Their music fills the quiet forest like happy laughter between best friends.
rationale: Stages the joyful love of the krauncha pair, the happiness soon to be broken.

title: The Cruel Arrow
on_slide_text: Suddenly a Nishada fowler lifts his bow with no anger and no reason. He lets the sharp arrow fly. The male bird falls, covered in red blood and shaking in pain. His mate cries out loudly, flapping and weeping for her lost love.
rationale: Stages the apex killing without cause and the mate's grief, the epic's spark.

title: The Curse of Sorrow
speaker: Valmiki
on_slide_text: O Nishada, you killed one of a loving pair lost in joy for no reason. You broke a happy song with cruel force. For this heartless act you shall never find honour or lasting glory. Learn that love must never be shot down.
rationale: Stages the compassionate curse where sorrow bursts as moral speech.

title: What Left My Mouth
speaker: Valmiki
on_slide_text: What words have just left my mouth? Look, Bharadwaja, these lines stand in equal feet and sweet rhythm. They can be sung to the veena's strings. Born from my deep sorrow, this new music shall be called a shloka for all time.
rationale: Stages the startled discovery of metre as shloka fit for veena.

title: Bath and Return
on_slide_text: Bharadwaja nods with joy and repeats the sweet verse back. Valmiki feels peace hearing his student's voice. He bathes in the clear water and walks back to his hut, still turning the rhythm in his mind. Bharadwaja follows behind with the full water pot.
rationale: Shows disciple support, bathing, and thoughtful return carrying the pitcher.

title: Brahma Arrives
on_slide_text: Back at his leaf hut Valmiki chats lightly about daily tasks. Yet inside his heart the new verse keeps beating again and again. Suddenly a bright light fills the air. Four-faced Brahma himself, glowing and kind, appears to meet the sage.
rationale: Brings the divine turn with Brahma's sudden arrival amid the echoing verse.

title: Welcoming Brahma
on_slide_text: The moment Valmiki sees Brahma he jumps up in wonder. He stands silent with folded hands and bows low. He washes Brahma's feet with clean water and offers a high seat. Brahma smiles warmly, asks about his health, and invites him to sit.
rationale: Shows reverent welcome and seating that honours Brahma.

title: Stuck in Sorrow
on_slide_text: Even seated beside Brahma, Valmiki cannot smile. His mind stays stuck on the sad riverbank. He keeps picturing the sweet bird singing before death. He thinks, what a heavy wrong that hunter did, taking a joyful life for no cause at all.
rationale: Shows Valmiki stuck in sorrow even before God, needing direction.

title: Write Rama's Story
speaker: Brahma
on_slide_text: Dear Valmiki, do not doubt, this new metre from your lips will live forever. By my wish it burst from your grief. Now use it to sing Rama's full story, with Lakshmana, Sita, and the rakshasas. All truth, seen and unseen, will shine to you, and no word will fail.
rationale: Stages Brahma's command to compose Rama's story in the immortal metre.

title: Living Beyond Mountains
on_slide_text: As long as high mountains and deep oceans stand on earth, your Ramayana will travel among people. As long as children sing this tale, you will live in my world and here. Saying this, Brahma vanishes, and Valmiki gazes in joyful wonder.
rationale: Stages the blessing of endurance and vanishing that seals authority.

title: Disciples Sing Again
on_slide_text: Valmiki's disciples clap and sing the new verse again and again. Four short lines, even beats, full of tender sadness. They laugh with hope and say, our teacher will now sing the whole Ramayana in this sweet singing style for the world.
rationale: Shows disciples repeating the verse and foreseeing the full Ramayana.

title: The Ramayana Is Born
on_slide_text: Blessed and bright, sage Valmiki sits to weave Rama's line in hundreds of sweet verses. He sings Rama, noblest of Raghus, and the fall of ten-headed Ravana in simple tuneful words. Here by still water and kind grief, the great Ramayana is born.
rationale: Closes on the resolving beat where the Ramayana is born in sweet shlokas.

title: Clear Mind Sees Pain
question: Why is Tamasa's clean bank like the mind of a good person?
answer: Because muddy water hides your face, and a busy mind hides another's pain. Valmiki wanted clean water to bathe, but he found clean sight to care. He could hear both happy song and sad cry. Sit ten quiet minutes each day with no screen, and you will see who is hurting near you.
on_slide_text: Why call Tamasa's clean bank like a good mind? Because muddy water hides your face, and a noisy mind hides others' pain. Valmiki found clean water and gained clean sight. Sit ten quiet minutes daily with no phone, and notice whose hurt you see first.
rationale: Pauses after the pure bank to draw the mind-clarity lesson from the reflection.

title: Curse Born of Love
question: Why does a holy book start with an angry curse instead of a sweet blessing?
answer: Because Valmiki's deep sorrow boiled over as hot anger, and hot anger cooled into lasting music. His curse was really love crying for broken joy. Loose pain stays heavy inside, but pain tied in rhythm turns into meaning. When anger burns you, write four short lines instead of shouting at someone.
on_slide_text: Why start a holy tale with a curse and not a blessing? Because deep sorrow first bursts out as hot anger, and anger is only love boiling over. Shaped pain turns into song that lasts. When anger burns you this week, write four short lines and make your own small shloka.
rationale: Reflects on curse-born compassion right after the outburst.

title: Do Not Break Play
question: Why was the hunter's everyday work called such a great wrong?
answer: Because he shot without hate and without need into singing love at play. Valmiki does not blame honest work, he blames breaking joy for fun. We do the same when we mock, cut off talk, or troll for laughs. Pause this week, notice your arrow, and choose kind silence instead.
on_slide_text: Why blame a hunter just doing his daily work? Because he shot without hate and without need into singing love at play. Breaking joy for fun is true cruelty. Watch this week where you mock or troll, and choose kind silence instead of shooting your arrow.
rationale: Reflects on causeless cruelty right after the killing.

title: Catch Your True Line
question: Why did wise Valmiki gasp at his own mouth?
answer: Because true songs come before we understand them. Valmiki did not build the beat, his grief sang it in even steps fit for veena. That fast flow runs ahead of slow thinking. He asked Bharadwaja to hold the line, for a new spark needs a friend's eyes. Write your true line at once and share it.
on_slide_text: Why did Valmiki gasp at his own mouth? Because true making comes first and knowing comes later. Grief sang an even beat by itself, like music flowing. New sparks fade fast. When a true line jumps from your heart this week, write it down at once and show a trusted friend.
rationale: Reflects on creation-before-understanding and witnessing the spark.

title: Turn Wound Into Work
question: Why did Brahma turn one bird's grief into Rama's huge story?
answer: Because a lonely hurt stays a small cry, but a blessed hurt becomes work for many. Brahma showed Valmiki his tears were for every parted love, like Sita parted from Rama. Truth seen with kindness lasts longer than mountains. Name one old hurt this week and use it to help one person.
on_slide_text: Why make one bird's grief into Rama and Sita's vast tale? Because a lonely wound stays a cry, but a blessed wound becomes work for all. Valmiki's tears were for every parted love. Name one old hurt this week and turn it into help for someone else.
rationale: Reflects on wound-into-work after the divine commission.
